section.title: Warning to the Rich
section.sectionRationale: James returns a final time to wealth, now not to warn the church against favoring the rich but to thunder against oppressive rich people themselves. In the voice of an Old Testament prophet he pronounces coming misery on those who hoard, defraud their workers, live in luxury, and condemn the righteous. Their rotting riches and unpaid wages testify against them before the Lord of Hosts.
section.thesis: Wealth hoarded and gained by fraud and injustice will rot and testify against its owners in the last days, for the cries of the defrauded reach the Lord of Hosts, who will judge the self-indulgent oppressors of the righteous.
section.frameNote: Two movements: corroded riches as a witness in the last days; and the withheld wages, luxury, and bloodshed that cry out to the Lord of Hosts.

units.label: Rotting riches, a witness against you
units.note: treasure hoarded in the last days

verses.text: Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you.
Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes.
Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have {{thesaurizo|hoarded treasure}} in the last days.

units.label: The cries that reach the Lord of Hosts

verses.text: Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the {{sabaoth|Lord of Hosts}}.
You have lived on earth in {{truphao|luxury}} and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter.
You have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you.

thesaurizo.gloss: To store up, hoard, lay up treasure. James charges the rich with hoarding wealth in the last days, the very time to be generous and ready for the Lord's coming. The word echoes Jesus' warning against laying up treasure on earth rather than treasure in heaven.

sabaoth.gloss: Hosts, armies; the Lord of Hosts, or Lord of Sabaoth, is the Lord who commands the armies of heaven. This transliterated Hebrew title portrays God as the all-powerful, sovereign King who hears the cries of the oppressed and marches to their defense. The defrauded laborers have this mighty Judge on their side.

truphao.gloss: To live in luxury, indulgence, and soft self-pleasing. James condemns the rich for a pampered life built on the suffering of others, fattening themselves like animals unaware of the day of slaughter. Such self-indulgence, feeding on injustice, ripens them for judgment.

basic.context: James suddenly sounds like an Old Testament prophet, thundering at rich oppressors. Weep and wail, he says, because misery is coming. Your hoarded wealth is already rotting, your fine clothes moth-eaten, your gold corroded, and that decay will be a witness against you. Worse, you cheated your workers, keeping back their pay, and those unpaid wages are crying out to God, the Lord of armies, who hears. You lived in luxury while others suffered, fattening yourselves for the day of slaughter, and you even condemned and killed the innocent, who did not fight back. It is a warning of certain judgment on wealth gained and used unjustly.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic denunciation, and it is important to see exactly what James condemns. He does not condemn wealth as such, but wealth hoarded, gained by fraud, spent on self-indulgence, and used to oppress the righteous. The rich addressed may include unbelieving oppressors outside the church, so this functions partly as comfort to the suffering poor: God sees, and He will judge. The last days language shows this is not merely ancient history but the present age before Christ's return.
basic.originalLanguages: The rich thesaurizo, hoard treasure, in the last days. Their victims' cries reach the sabaoth, the Lord of Hosts, the God of armies. And they live in truphao, luxury and self-indulgence, fattening themselves for slaughter. The words move from hoarding to the cry of the oppressed to a doomed life of ease.
basic.typology: The prophetic woe against oppressive wealth echoes Amos and Isaiah and points forward to the final judgment of Babylon the great in Revelation, where the merchants' riches come to nothing. The righteous who did not resist, condemned and murdered, foreshadows Christ, the ultimate righteous One who did not resist those who condemned Him.
basic.christ: The righteous one who is condemned and murdered yet does not resist points powerfully to Jesus, who like a lamb was led to slaughter and opened not His mouth. The Lord of Hosts who hears the cries of the oppressed is the God who vindicates His Son and all who suffer in Him. And Jesus' own warnings against hoarding treasure and His blessing on the poor stand behind this passage.
basic.god: God is the Lord of Hosts, the almighty King who hears the cries of the defrauded and the oppressed and will surely act. He is the righteous Judge before whom hoarded wealth becomes evidence and unpaid wages become an accusation. He is not indifferent to injustice; He sees the luxury of the powerful and the suffering of the weak, and He will set the account right.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus warned against laying up treasure on earth, Matthew 6:19-21, and about the danger of riches, Luke 6:24. The withheld wages recall Deuteronomy 24:14-15 and Malachi 3:5. The Lord of Hosts hearing the oppressed echoes Isaiah 5:9. And Revelation 18 depicts the fall of luxurious Babylon.
basic.oneStory: The prophets thundered against the rich who trampled the poor, and God always heard the cry of the oppressed, from Israel groaning in Egypt to the harvesters cheated of their wages. James takes up that prophetic voice in the last days, warning that hoarded, unjust wealth will testify against its owners before the Lord of Hosts. The righteous who suffer without resisting share the path of Christ, the true righteous One, and await the day when the Judge who hears every cry will make all things right.

context.literary:
James 5:1 to 6 is a single sustained oracle, and it is the only passage in the New Testament letters written wholly in the register of the Hebrew prophets. It opens with the same two Greek words as 4:13, 'Come now', but the tone has changed. The merchants of chapter 4 were lectured, and the rich of chapter 5 are summoned to be sentenced. The command that begins the oracle is a pair of imperatives, 'weep and wail', and the second is the prophets' word for the howling that accompanies a day of judgment, as in Isaiah 13:6. Nothing is said about repentance. No promise of grace is offered in these six verses, and that silence is part of the literary effect.

The oracle has two panels. Verses 2 and 3 are about things: riches, clothes, gold and silver, and what happens to them. Verses 4 to 6 are about people: the workers whose wages were kept back, the poor who were crushed, the righteous one who was killed. The first panel is a charge delivered by objects, the second by victims. In both, the accusation comes in the perfect tense, 'have rotted', 'have been withheld', 'have lived', 'have condemned', so that the sentence is presented as already written.

The three charges are arranged as a slope from the passive to the active. First comes hoarding, which harms no one by itself. Then comes fraud, which actively harms the worker. Then comes the climax, murder of the righteous. The same slope appears in Isaiah 5:8 to 10 and Amos 8:4 to 6.

Two other things stand out. The word for the 'misery' in verse 1 comes from the same root as the command to 'grieve' in 4:9, and the passage gains force when read against it: those who refused to be wretched in repentance will be wretched in judgment. The second is that verse 6 ends in a short, hard sentence without a conclusion, 'He does not resist you'. The abrupt close leaves the reader with the silence of the victim, which is where the oracle wants us.
context.historical:
The economic world behind the passage was agrarian and unequal. In first century Palestine much of the land was held in large estates, and a great deal of the work was done by hired labourers who were paid by the day. A day labourer lived close to the edge, and a day's wages bought the day's food. For that reason the Law said 'You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand', Leviticus 19:13, and 'You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them', Deuteronomy 24:15. Jesus' parable of the labourers in the vineyard assumes that pay is due at evening, Matthew 20:8. To keep wages back was not a delay in accounts but a threat to a family's survival.

The prophets had condemned the same social pattern in earlier centuries. Isaiah condemned those who 'add house to house and join field to field', Isaiah 5:8, and said the plunder of the poor was in their houses, Isaiah 3:14 and 15. Amos described merchants who cheated 'with dishonest scales' and 'buy the poor with silver', Amos 8:5 and 6. Jeremiah said 'Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness... who makes his countrymen serve without pay', Jeremiah 22:13, and Malachi included 'those who defraud laborers of their wages' among those the Lord would judge, Malachi 3:5. James stands in that line.

Wealth was held in forms that rot. Stored grain could spoil, fine garments were a standard form of savings, and Scripture treats them as such: Achan took a beautiful cloak along with silver and gold, Joshua 7:21. Silver and gold do not rust, but corrode and tarnish, and a hoard that is never used is a hoard that is not doing what money is for. James's pictures were ordinary pictures of what happens to unused treasure, and the poor in his audience knew them.

The addressees are not necessarily members of the church. James has already reminded his readers that the rich oppressed them and dragged them into court, 2:6, and his readers may be listening to the oracle against their oppressors. The language of 'the last days' places the whole scene in the age inaugurated by Christ's coming and awaiting His return, as Acts 2:17 and Hebrews 1:2 use the phrase.
context.canonical:
Behind the paragraph stands a century of prophecy. The decisive line in the Law is that God hears the cry of the poor: 'If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry', Exodus 22:23, and Deuteronomy 24:15 says the unpaid labourer 'may cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin'. Even the first murder produced a cry, Genesis 4:10: 'The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground.' James is invoking the oldest legal and moral principle in Scripture, that injustice makes a sound that God hears.

The title 'the Lord of Hosts', a transliteration of Hebrew tsebaoth, is the prophetic name for God in His role as king of armies, and it is the name Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah and Malachi use when He speaks in judgment on injustice, Isaiah 3:15, Zechariah 7:9 and 10, Malachi 3:5. The name appears in the New Testament here and in Romans 9:29 where Paul quotes Isaiah. James is deliberately putting the oppressed in the care of the God who commands the armies of heaven.

Jesus supplies the New Testament counterpart. 'Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy', Matthew 6:19, is almost the same picture, and 'woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort', Luke 6:24. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus, Luke 16:19 to 25, shows a rich man whose fault was not violence but neglect, and Matthew 25:41 to 45 makes the same point about the least of these. Paul's counsel to Timothy about the rich, 1 Timothy 6:9, 10 and 17 to 19, offers a way out: not to put hope in uncertain wealth, to be generous, and to treasure up 'a firm foundation for the future'.

The 'righteous one' in verse 6 is also a New Testament title for Christ, Acts 3:14 and 7:52. The idea that the righteous suffer at the hands of the powerful is a pattern running from Abel through the prophets to the cross, and Isaiah 53:7 describes the silent sufferer who 'did not open His mouth'.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
James intends to do two things at once, and they pull in opposite directions. He means to terrify the powerful, and he means to comfort the powerless. The oracle is addressed to the rich in the second person, but it is overheard by the poor in the congregation, and the second purpose is as real as the first. Believers who had been cheated and dragged to court needed to hear that their loss was seen by the Lord of Hosts and that the books are not closed.

The first purpose requires him to speak without hedging. He does not offer the rich a programme of repentance here. That is a deliberate choice: in a letter that elsewhere teaches grace to sinners, he lets this one passage stand as pure warning. His readers are meant to feel what a prophet's word of judgment feels like when it lands on a person who has been comfortable.

He also intends to show his readers what wealth does to a person. The riches are not merely in danger; they have become evidence. Hoarded gold and unpaid wages are not neutral facts but witnesses. A reader who has any wealth, large or small, is invited to ask what his possessions would say if they were called to testify.

Finally, the oracle prepares for what follows. The next verses call the oppressed to patient endurance until the Lord's coming, 5:7 and 8. They can wait without bitterness because the Judge is real. James wants his readers to leave this passage not planning revenge but trusting the God who has already heard.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The oracle describes particular sins and announces judgment on those who commit them, and it does not command anything of its hearers directly except to weep and wail. Its commands are implied by its accusations: pay what is owed, do not hoard, do not live in luxury at the expense of others, do not take advantage of those who cannot resist. The Law had said all of this already, and James is applying it rather than adding to it.

It is important to see what is not being said. James does not say that wealth is evil, that every rich person is guilty, or that believers must give up all possessions. The accusations are specific: wealth that was hoarded, wages that were withheld, luxury that was bought with someone else's labour, and violence against the righteous. Reading the passage as a general condemnation of prosperity misses the target, and reading it as a comfort for the comfortable misses it more badly.

For modern readers the passage applies in ordinary ways. Employers, landlords, shareholders and consumers all have some connection to the pay and conditions of those who work for them, and the Law's concern about wages due before sunset speaks to delayed invoices, unpaid overtime and underpaid domestic or farm work. The passage also warns anyone who has savings that are never used for good. For those who are on the receiving end of injustice, it gives permission to cry out to God and to trust that the cry is heard, without taking judgment into their own hands.

debates.question: Does James condemn wealth itself, or its misuse?

views.label: The misuse of wealth, not wealth as such
views.case: James targets specific sins: hoarding, fraud against workers, self-indulgent luxury, and oppression of the righteous. Scripture elsewhere includes godly wealthy believers, and James earlier honored the poor without demonizing all riches. The woe falls on unjust acquisition and use, not on possessing money.

views.label: A sweeping prophetic woe on the rich as a class
views.case: Others note how absolute the language is, addressed simply to you who are rich, in the tradition of prophetic woes and Jesus' woe to the rich in Luke 6:24. On this reading it is a stark warning about the spiritual peril of riches in general.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage sounds a grave warning about wealth. The consistent biblical witness is that riches are perilous and must be held justly and generously, or they become a witness against their owner.

debates.question: Who are the rich being addressed?

views.label: Oppressors outside the church
views.case: The rich here defraud workers, live in luxury, and murder the righteous, matching the wealthy oppressors of chapter 2 who dragged believers to court. On this view James addresses them prophetically while comforting the oppressed believers who overhear.

views.label: A warning also to any wealthy within the church
views.case: Others hold the warning reaches wealthy members too, pressing every rich believer to examine whether their wealth is hoarded or unjustly used. The last days horizon makes it a live warning for all.

debates.bearing: Whether aimed chiefly at outside oppressors or at any rich hearer, the effect is the same: God will judge unjust wealth, and the oppressed can trust that He hears.

debates.question: Who is the righteous one who does not resist in verse 6?

views.label: Righteous people in general, the poor who were defrauded and killed
views.case: The article may be generic, as in 'the righteous' of the Psalms and Proverbs. James has just described exploited labourers and earlier spoke of the poor being dragged into court. On this reading 'he does not resist you' describes how the victims, lacking power, simply took it, and it prepares for the call to patient endurance in 5:7 to 11.

views.label: Christ, the Righteous One
views.case: Acts uses the title for Jesus, Acts 3:14 and 7:52, and the silent victim echoes Isaiah 53:7. Some therefore see a deliberate allusion, with James accusing the rich as members of the class that crucified the Lord. The strength of the view is the title and the pattern. Its weakness is that James nowhere else makes the allusion explicit.

views.label: A question about God: 'Does He not oppose you?'
views.case: The verb is the one James used in 4:6, 'God opposes the proud', and the Greek clause could be read as a question. The oracle would then end with God drawn up against the oppressors. The weakness is that the subject changes abruptly without a signal in the Greek.

debates.bearing: On each reading the verse leaves the oppressors facing a judge. Whether the victim is a poor believer, the Lord Himself or the Lord's retort, the call for believers is the same: do not retaliate, and trust that the cry has been heard.

study.originalLanguages:
The oracle opens with klausate ololyzontes, 'weep, howling'. The second word is ololyzo, a word that sounds like what it means. It is the prophets' verb for the cry of grief at the day of judgment in the Greek Old Testament, as in Isaiah 13:6, 'Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near'. James uses it once, and by choosing it he tells his readers that this is the voice of the prophets, not the voice of a moralist.

The 'misery' of verse 1 is talaiporia, from the root of the verb used in 4:9, 'Grieve', the command to be wretched in repentance. James's logic is plain: the repentance he asked for there would have spared them the wretchedness here. In both places the word means a kind of wretched suffering, in one case chosen and in the other imposed.

In verse 2 the two verbs 'have rotted' (sesepen) and 'have become moth-eaten' (sesametobrota) are both in the perfect tense. The perfect describes a past action whose result stands. The riches are already in a state of ruin. This could be a statement of what has literally happened to stored goods, or a prophetic perfect in which the future judgment is spoken of as done. The text allows both, and it may mean both: the hoard that is hoarded is already spoiled by being hoarded.

Verse 3 speaks of gold and silver as 'corroded', and the noun for the corrosion is ios. The same word appears in James 3:8, where the tongue is 'full of deadly poison', and in Romans 3:13, 'the venom of vipers'. Ios therefore means both rust and poison, and the passage can be heard on both registers: the money has a poison in it. 'Testify' is martyrion, a witness in a legal case, so the rust is a witness for the prosecution. 'Consume your flesh like fire' can also be divided so that 'like fire' joins the next sentence, 'You have hoarded fire in the last days', but the BSB's reading is the most natural. 'Hoarded treasure' is thesaurizo, to store up a thesaurus, and the verb is the same word as the one Jesus uses in Matthew 6:19 and 20, 'store up'. The people who stored up treasure on earth have, in the end, stored up the wrong thing.

The 'wages withheld' in verse 4 translates a participle in the perfect passive which means the wages are in a state of having been taken away, and the verb 'cry out' (krazo) is in the present tense. The cry is going on now. 'Lord of Hosts' is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew, kyriou sabaoth, and it appears in the New Testament only here and Romans 9:29. The phrase 'reached the ears' is literally 'entered into the ears', and the passage puts the cry of the poor in the ears of the one who commands the armies.

In verse 5 'lived in luxury' is truphao, a word found only here in the New Testament, from the family of words for softness and indulgence. 'Self-indulgence' is spatalao, a word Paul uses of the widow who lives for pleasure in 1 Timothy 5:6, the one who is 'dead even while she is still alive'. The tense is aorist, a summary of their whole life. The phrase 'fattened your hearts' is an image of animals being made ready for slaughter, and it echoes Jeremiah 12:3, where the wicked are dragged away 'like sheep to the slaughter', and Deuteronomy 32:15, where Jeshurun 'grew fat and kicked'. 'In the day of slaughter' may be the day of their feasting or the day of their doom, and the double meaning is probably deliberate.

Verse 6 says 'the righteous' in the singular, with the article, and 'does not resist' translates ouk antitassetai, which is exactly the verb of 4:6, where 'God opposes the proud'. Some read the clause as a question, 'Does He not oppose you?', with God as the subject, so that the verse ends with the Lord arrayed against the killers. Most take it as a statement about the victim: he did not resist. The linguistic link to 4:6 is real in both cases.

typology.type: The righteous one who does not resist
typology.fulfillment: Verse 6 speaks of a righteous victim who 'did not resist', and the whole line from Abel to the prophets is the pattern behind it. It finds its fulfilment in Christ, 'the Holy and Righteous One' whom the people killed, Acts 3:14, and of whom Isaiah wrote that He was 'led like a lamb to the slaughter' and 'did not open His mouth', Isaiah 53:7. Peter says 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate', 1 Peter 2:23. The type is incomplete in earlier sufferers, who were wronged but not sinless and whose deaths did not redeem; only the cross turns the innocent blood into a sacrifice for the guilty.

Abel's blood cried out from the ground, Genesis 4:10, and Israel's groaning in Egypt reached God, Exodus 3:7. James draws on both when the wages cry out and reach the ears of the Lord of Hosts. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ's blood, which Hebrews says 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel', Hebrews 12:24. Abel's blood called for vengeance; the blood of Jesus calls for mercy. The type falls short because the earlier cries asked for justice against particular wrongdoers, while the cry of Christ's blood is the ground on which even the wrongdoers can be forgiven.

typology.type: Treasure that rots and treasure that lasts
typology.fulfillment: Hoarded wealth that spoils is a repeated image in the wisdom writings and the prophets, and Jesus sets it against 'treasures in heaven', Matthew 6:19 and 20. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, who is Himself the treasure in the field, Matthew 13:44, and who gave everything: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor', 2 Corinthians 8:9. Believers who are told to be 'rich in good works' have an inheritance 'that can never perish, spoil or fade', 1 Peter 1:4. The type does not cover how the poor share in the treasure, and so it needs the gospel to complete it.

typology.type: The day of the Lord as a day of slaughter
typology.fulfillment: The prophets used the day of slaughter as the day when God settles accounts with the unjust, Jeremiah 12:3 and Zephaniah 1:18. It points forward to the day of Christ's return, when 'the Judge is standing at the door', James 5:9, and when the nations will be judged by the Son of Man, Matthew 25:31 to 46. It is not yet completely fulfilled, and the passage's 'last days' language places believers between the first and second comings. The type is held open until the day when every cry has been answered.

study.christ:
The oracle leads to Christ first by the figure of the righteous one. James 5:6 does not name him, but the singular with the article reads like a title, and in the sermons of Acts the apostles use that very title of Jesus: 'You rejected the Holy and Righteous One', Acts 3:14, and Stephen says the fathers 'killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One', Acts 7:52. Whether or not James intended the verse to point at the cross, the pattern fits it exactly. A just man is condemned and killed by people with power, and does not resist. Isaiah 53:7 and 1 Peter 2:23 describe the same silence. Whoever reads the verse in the light of Good Friday hears more in it than a sentence about the poor.

It leads to Christ by contrast. The rich of the oracle have stored treasure for the last days, and Christ is the one who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor', 2 Corinthians 8:9. The oppressors take wages from labourers; Christ pays a debt He did not owe. They fatten themselves for slaughter; He is led as a lamb to it. They kill the innocent; He gives His life for the guilty. Luke's gospel presents Him as announcing good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, and Mary's song anticipates the day when He 'has sent the rich away empty', Luke 1:53.

It leads to Christ as the Judge. The Lord of Hosts hears the cries of the harvesters, and the New Testament says the Father has given judgment to the Son, John 5:22. James will say a few verses later that 'the Judge is standing at the door', James 5:9. When Jesus speaks of the end in Matthew 25, the king who divides the sheep from the goats identifies Himself with the hungry and the stranger: 'whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me', Matthew 25:45. The poor workers of James 5:4 are, in that light, people Christ has taken as His own.

It leads to Christ as the one who can change the rich. The rich man in Luke 19, Zacchaeus, met Jesus and said 'half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold', Luke 19:8. The passage in James offers no repentance, but the Gospels show that it is possible. Jesus says it is 'hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven', Matthew 19:23, and adds that 'with God all things are possible', Matthew 19:26. The oracle's severity is not a final word on any individual rich person, only on a life that stays in its hoard.

We should be careful not to turn the passage into an allegory. The rust and moths are not types of the cross. But the passage is a faithful, if harsh, piece of the same prophetic voice that Jesus claimed, and every line of it finds its answer in Him.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who hears. This is the central statement of the paragraph and one of the deepest claims in Scripture about the divine character. The cries of the harvesters 'have reached the ears' of the Lord of Hosts. God is not a distant force indifferent to the arrangements of the market. He hears the labourer whose employer is far away and whose complaint no court will take up. It is the same God who said to Moses 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors', Exodus 3:7. The doctrine that God knows and cares is here a concrete and local fact about particular wages.

It shows a God who rules as the Lord of Hosts. The title in the Old Testament is the name of the one who commands heaven's armies, and James uses it in the one paragraph where the powerless most need the strongest ally. The point is not that God is on the side of the poor because they are poor, but that He is just, and that no power on earth is beyond His reach. The rich are used to being able to buy influence. They cannot buy the Lord of Hosts.

It shows a God who is just in a way that includes wealth. The justice of God in this passage is not abstract. It concerns pay slips, harvests, courts and meals. A doctrine of God that left out economics would leave out most of life, and the Law, the prophets and James insist that God is concerned with fair weights, fair wages and honest dealing, Leviticus 19:13 and Micah 6:8.

It shows a God who judges at a time of His choosing. The 'last days' mean that judgment has been set but not yet executed, and the next verses call believers to patience. This is the tension James holds together: the Lord hears now and will act in His time, and the believer must wait. The delay is not indifference. Peter says the Lord is patient 'not wanting anyone to perish', 2 Peter 3:9, and the same patience that gives the rich time to repent is the patience the oppressed must exercise.

It shows a God whose judgment is not blind to what a person is. He knows the heart that was 'fattened'. He also knows the one who was killed and did not resist, and He does not forget him. Psalm 34:18 says the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.

For worship, the passage invites a kind of confidence and a kind of fear. Confidence belongs to those who have been wronged and may rest in a God who sees. Fear belongs to those who have profited at others' expense and need to know that nothing is hidden. Together they make for honest worship: giving thanks that there is a Judge, and asking Him to make us people who do not need to be judged this way.

crossReferences.note: Pay the poor labourer his wages each day before sunset, or he may cry out to the LORD against you and you will be guilty of sin. This is the law behind James 5:4, and it shows that the withheld wages are a breach of a commandment as well as an unkindness, with a promise that the cry will be heard.

You must not defraud your neighbour or withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand. It sits in the chapter that also commands love for the neighbour as oneself, and it shows that James's charge of fraud is rooted in the same law that James elsewhere calls royal.

The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground. The first murder produced the first cry that God heard, and James draws on that pattern for the crying of the wages and the silent killing of the righteous in verse 6.

If you mistreat the widow or the orphan and they cry out, I will surely hear their cry. It is a direct statement of the principle that drives James 5:4, that God personally listens to the cry of the vulnerable and treats their mistreatment as an offence against Himself.

Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field. The oracle goes on to say the Lord of Hosts has declared many houses will become desolate. The woe of land hoarders and the title of the Lord of Hosts are both here, showing that James's paragraph is the voice of Isaiah.

Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness, who makes his countrymen serve without pay and fails to pay their wages. It is the prophetic version of the charge in James 5:4, and shows that unpaid labour was a mark of the kind of ruler God condemned.

Hear this, you who trample the needy and cheat with dishonest scales. Amos describes merchants who treat the poor as property. It parallels James's picture of exploitation and gives the historical background for the fatal slope from fraud to the death of the righteous.

Do not store up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy. The saying of Jesus is the nearest parallel to verses 2 and 3, and shows that James is applying his Lord's teaching in the strong tones of a prophet.

Woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort. It is Jesus' own woe, and the same note of reversal. James is not inventing a harsh word; he is repeating a woe the Master had spoken, and adding concrete reasons.

Paul tells Timothy to instruct the rich not to be conceited or hope in uncertain wealth, but to do good and be generous. It is the constructive counterpart of James's warning, showing that the right use of wealth exists and is described in the New Testament.

Peter says the people rejected the Holy and Righteous One. Whether or not James has Jesus in view in verse 6, the apostolic preaching uses the title in the same way, and it makes the death of the righteous one the climax of the world's injustice.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with a good creation and a human race given dominion to care for it, Genesis 1:28. Wealth in the beginning is the abundance of the garden, and work is a gift. The fall twists that gift. The first sins of the new world are theft of what was forbidden, blame of the neighbour, and then murder over a brother's offering. When God says that Abel's blood cries out from the ground, He establishes an important principle for everything that follows: no injustice is silent.

The law at Sinai then turns that principle into a system of care. It orders wages, gleanings, loans, sabbath rests and the year of release, all so that a poor person has a place in the community. The prophets accuse Israel of dismantling that system. They said the Lord of Hosts is watching the field and the scale, and that the day of the Lord would be darkness for those who thought they were safe. Their message in Isaiah, Amos, Jeremiah and Malachi is James 5 in other voices.

In Christ the story pivots. The one who is the true heir of all things becomes poor, announces good news to the poor, and takes the cry of the oppressed into His own mouth on the cross. The righteous One is killed without resisting, and God raises Him, which means that the death of the innocent is not the last word. His people are told to be rich in good works, to share, and to hold their possessions loosely. The church becomes the place where the wealthy and the poor sit down together, which is why James is so severe on favouritism earlier in the letter.

The ending of the story is the reversal that the oracle announces. In Revelation 18 the merchants weep over a fallen city whose wealth was built on the exploitation of others, and the cries of the saints are answered, Revelation 6:10 and 19:2. The new creation is a place where nothing rots, nothing is stolen, and no worker is cheated, where the poor inherit the kingdom and the Lord wipes away every tear. Until then, the church waits as the farmer waits, with patience that is not passivity, trusting that the Judge is at the door, and doing now what it can to see that the wages are paid.

quiz.q: What does James say will happen to the hoarded riches of the wicked?

options.text: They rot and corrode, becoming a witness that testifies against their owners.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3: the decayed wealth itself condemns them.

options.text: Their gold and silver corrode and will consume their flesh like fire.
options.note: True to verse 3, vivid imagery of the same judgment.

options.text: They will be safely preserved for future generations.
options.note: The opposite: the riches rot and testify against them.

options.text: They will guarantee the owners' security before God.
options.note: Hoarded wealth becomes evidence against them, not security.

quiz.q: What sin against workers does James highlight in verse 4?

options.text: Withholding the wages of the harvesters, whose cries reach the Lord of Hosts.
options.note: Verse 4: defrauded wages cry out to the almighty Judge.

options.text: Cheating laborers of pay they depended on to live.
options.note: True to the sense, naming the injustice involved.

options.text: Paying workers slightly late on occasion.
options.note: The charge is withholding wages outright, a grave injustice.

options.text: Giving workers too much rest.
options.note: The sin is exploitation, not generosity toward workers.

quiz.q: Does this passage condemn all wealth or its misuse?

options.text: It condemns hoarding, fraud, luxury, and oppression, the misuse of wealth.
options.note: The specific sins named are unjust acquisition and use, not mere possession.

options.text: It sounds a sweeping prophetic woe on the peril of riches.
options.note: True to the stark tone, echoing Jesus' woe to the rich.

options.text: It teaches that money is entirely neutral and never dangerous.
options.note: Scripture and James both warn of the real peril of riches.

options.text: It commands believers to become wealthy.
options.note: The passage warns the rich, it does not commend pursuing riches.

quiz.q: Who is the Lord of Hosts in verse 4?

options.text: The almighty God, commander of heaven's armies, who hears the oppressed.
options.note: The title portrays God as sovereign King and defender of the wronged.

options.text: The mighty Judge on the side of the defrauded laborers.
options.note: True to the comfort in the title, if less full than its meaning.

options.text: A minor angelic figure with limited power.
options.note: The title names God Himself as Lord of the heavenly armies.

options.text: An impersonal force indifferent to human affairs.
options.note: He personally hears and will act on the cries of the oppressed.

quiz.q: How does the description of the righteous in verse 6 point beyond itself?

options.text: The righteous condemned and murdered, not resisting, foreshadows Christ.
options.note: It echoes the Righteous One led like a lamb to slaughter, Isaiah 53.

options.text: It pictures innocent sufferers who do not fight back against injustice.
options.note: True to the immediate sense, the pattern fulfilled in Jesus.

options.text: It shows that the righteous always triumph immediately in this life.
options.note: Here the righteous suffer now; vindication comes from the Judge.

options.text: It teaches that the righteous deserve their suffering.
options.note: They are innocent, oppressed by the unjust rich.

questions: James warns against hoarding wealth in the last days. Where might you be storing up for yourself rather than being generous and ready for the Lord's coming?
God hears the cries of cheated workers. Are there people whose labor you benefit from who are treated unjustly, and how might you respond?
The rich fattened their hearts in luxury while others suffered. How can comfort and plenty dull us to the needs of the poor around us?
This passage assures the oppressed that the Lord of Hosts hears them. Where do you need to trust that God sees an injustice done to you or to others?
The righteous who suffered without resisting point to Christ. How does His unjust suffering and vindication shape the way you bear wrongs done to you?

translationNotes.note: Hoarded treasure renders thesaurizo, to store up; the BSB prints a line break within the verse before You have hoarded treasure, which is set here as running prose.
Lord of Hosts renders Lord Sabaoth, a transliterated Hebrew title for the Lord of the heavenly armies, stressing God's power to defend the oppressed.
Luxury renders truphao, to live in soft self-indulgence; fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter pictures unwitting animals being readied for judgment.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for James 5:1-6. A line break within verse 3 is set as running prose.
